standard.title: Angles as turns
standard.description: identify angles as measures of turn and compare angles with right angles in everyday situations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify, describe and demonstrate quarter, half, three-quarter and full measures of turn in everyday situations (AC9M2M05). They have not yet formally defined these turns as angles or compared general angles to a right angle benchmark.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify angles as measures of turn and compare everyday angles with right angles.

nodes.label: Angle as a measure of turn
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain that an angle measures the amount of turn between two directions, and identify quarter, half and full turns as angles.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate quarter and half turns physically; identify these as angles and connect them to the corner of a square (right angle) and a straight line.
nodes.typical_width: Connect quarter turn to right angle, half turn to straight angle, and full turn to 360°; identify these angles in everyday objects and situations.
wider: Explore how turns are used in navigation and robotics — programming a simple floor robot to make quarter, half and three-quarter turns
Investigate how First Nations Australian dances and ceremonies use directional turns, connecting to angle measurement

response_modes.reason: Students often see angles only as static corners in shapes and miss the dynamic 'turn' definition. Encountering angles in movement contexts (physical turns, robotics, dance) establishes the measure-of-turn concept more broadly.

nodes.hinge_reason: The 'angle as turn' definition is the conceptual foundation for Node 2 — students who retain the 'angles are static corners' misconception cannot reliably classify angles relative to a right angle benchmark, because they have no dynamic reference point for what a right angle represents as a turn.
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The robotics and navigation context connects angle to programming and real-world direction, offering enrichment that extends beyond the immediate descriptor and has strong cross-curricular value.
success_criteria: Students can identify a right angle in an everyday context and explain it as a quarter turn.
Students can physically demonstrate a quarter, half and full turn and name each as an angle.

nodes.label: Comparing angles with right angles
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can classify everyday angles as equal to, greater than, or less than a right angle.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify three everyday angles (doors, corners, open books) as greater than, less than, or equal to a right angle; justify each classification.
nodes.typical_width: Compare a range of everyday angles with a right angle benchmark using a right angle tester; classify as acute (less than), right (equal to) or obtuse (greater than).
wider: Explore how right angles are used in construction and design — identifying right angles in building structures and why they are important
Introduce informal angle language (acute, obtuse) as natural extensions of the 'less than right angle / greater than right angle' description
success_criteria: Students can classify an angle as less than, equal to, or greater than a right angle.
Students can identify right angles in everyday environments using a right angle tester.
